systems-20.correctAnswer: A stack value cannot safely outlive its function because its frame is popped when the function returns: allocation and freeing are just moving the stack pointer in strict last-in-first-out order, so the memory is immediately available to be reused by the next call. A heap value can outlive its function because it is allocated explicitly and lives until it is explicitly freed or collected, independent of any function's frame, so a pointer to it remains valid across many calls as long as it has not been freed.
systems-20.question: In your own words, why can a stack value not safely outlive its function, and why can a heap value?

systems-20.correctAnswer: Recursing without a base case pushes a new stack frame on every call, with no return to pop them, so the stack grows until it collides with its limit or the heap and the program crashes with a stack overflow. Allocating in a loop without freeing grows the heap instead: each block is requested and never returned, so memory use climbs steadily, the system slows as memory fills, and eventually the process may be killed or the system may run out of memory. The first is a fast, visible crash; the second is a slow leak.
systems-20.question: Predict what happens when a program recurses without a base case, and when it allocates in a loop without freeing.

systems-20.correctAnswer: Pointers. A pointer is an address naming a location in memory, so a program can refer to a value in the stack or the heap without copying it, and can keep referring to a heap value long after the function that allocated it has returned. The next lesson is about that mechanism: what a pointer is, how dereferencing works, and what goes wrong when the thing at the address is no longer what you think it is.
systems-20.question: Connect this to the next lesson: if values live at addresses in these regions, what is the mechanism for referring to them?

systems-20-lab.correctAnswer: Draw a process image with a stack at one end and a heap at the other, growing towards each other. Stack frames, from bottom to top: main, then f called by main, then g called by f, each frame holding its return address, saved registers, and local variables. Plus one heap block, separate from the stack, allocated explicitly. Mark survival: when g returns, g's frame is popped and its locals die, but f's frame, main's frame, and the heap block survive. When f returns, f's frame is popped and its locals die, but main's frame and the heap block survive. When main returns, main's frame is popped and the process ends; the heap block survives only until it is explicitly freed, and if it is never freed it leaks. The key point is lifetime, not size: stack values die with their frame, heap values die only when freed.
systems-20-lab.question: Draw a process image with stack frames for main calling f calling g, plus one heap block. Label each value's region, and mark which values survive when g returns, when f returns, and when main returns.

systems-21.correctAnswer: A pointer is an address written on a card: a small value stored somewhere that names a location. The address is the street address itself, the number naming a byte in the process's address space. The value at that address is what lives in the house at that address: the data you find when you dereference the pointer and visit that location. Confusing any two of the three, or following a card after the house has been demolished, is where pointer bugs come from.
systems-21.question: In your own words, distinguish a pointer, an address, and the value at that address, using the house-and-card analogy or your own.

systems-21.correctAnswer: Returning a pointer to a stack local gives the caller a dangling pointer: the function's frame was popped on return, so that memory is free to be reused by the next call, and the value it held may change by itself or be overwritten, even though the pointer still looks valid. Keeping a pointer to a heap block after it is freed is the same kind of dangling pointer, called use-after-free: the block may be reallocated to other data, so reading or writing through the old pointer reads or corrupts data that now belongs to something else, with no error at the point of the mistake.
systems-21.question: Predict what happens when a function returns a pointer to its stack local, and when a heap block is freed but its pointer is kept.

systems-21.correctAnswer: By laying out many values together, using the same address arithmetic. An array lays out elements of the same type back-to-back, so element i is at base plus i times element size. A struct lays out fields of mixed types in declaration order, with padding so each field starts at a suitably aligned address. The next lesson is about that layout: how arrays and structs are arranged in memory, and what padding and alignment do to size and speed.
systems-21.question: Connect this to the next lesson: if a pointer names one element, how does a program lay out many elements, and structures of mixed types, in memory?

systems-21-lab.correctAnswer: Draw three variables in a row, each with its own address, and a pointer variable whose value is the address of the second variable. Show three things separately: the pointer itself, stored somewhere, the address it holds, which is the second variable's address, and the value at that address, which is the second variable's contents. When the pointer is incremented by one element, it moves by the size of one element, not by one byte, so it now points at the third variable, and dereferencing it gives the third variable's value. When the pointed-to value is freed, the pointer becomes dangling: it still holds the old address, but that memory no longer belongs to the original value and may be reused, so dereferencing it is unsafe.
systems-21-lab.question: On paper, draw three variables and a pointer to the second. Show the pointer, its address, and the value at that address. Then show what changes when the pointer is incremented by one element, and when the pointed-to value is freed.

systems-22.correctAnswer: The fifth element is at address 1032, assuming the first element is at address 1000. The address of element i is base plus i times element size, and the fifth element is index 4, counting from zero, so 1000 plus 4 times 8 equals 1032. If you count the first element as element 1 in words, that is still the same calculation: four steps of 8 bytes past the base.
systems-22.question: In your own words, compute the address of the fifth element of an array of 8-byte values starting at address 1000.

systems-22.correctAnswer: Without padding, the size is 6 bytes: 1 for the first byte, plus 4 for the integer, plus 1 for the last byte. With padding, the size is 12 bytes: the first byte at offset 0, three padding bytes at offsets 1 to 3 so the 4-byte integer starts at a multiple of 4, the integer at offsets 4 to 7, the last byte at offset 8, and three trailing padding bytes at offsets 9 to 11 so the whole struct size is a multiple of its largest alignment, 4. The two orders differ because padding depends on where the large field sits: byte, byte, integer needs only two padding bytes before the integer, for a total of 8, and integer, byte, byte needs two trailing padding bytes, also for a total of 8, while byte, integer, byte wastes padding both before the integer and at the end, for a total of 12. Reordering from largest to smallest therefore shrinks the struct.
systems-22.question: Predict the size of a struct with a byte, a 4-byte integer, and a byte, with and without padding — and explain why the two orders differ.

systems-22.correctAnswer: Two things go wrong, both because layout is predictable. If a program lives longer than its data, it can hold a pointer to memory that has already been freed or whose stack frame has been popped, and that dangling pointer will read or write memory that now belongs to something else. If a program writes beyond its bounds, it writes past the end of an array or struct into whatever follows it in memory, such as another variable, a saved register, or a return address, corrupting that neighbour silently. The next lesson is about those lifetime and bounds errors: use-after-free, double-free, leaks, and buffer overflows.
systems-22.question: Connect this to the next lesson: if layout is this predictable, what goes wrong when a program lives longer than its data, or writes beyond its bounds?

systems-22-lab.correctAnswer: Assume age is a 4-byte integer, grade average is an 8-byte double, and a pointer is 8 bytes, as the task specifies 8-byte alignment for pointers and doubles. Original order, name pointer, age, grade average: pointer at offsets 0 to 7, age at offsets 8 to 11, four padding bytes at offsets 12 to 15 so the double starts at a multiple of 8, double at offsets 16 to 23, total size 24. Reordered to minimise padding, pointer, double, age: pointer at offsets 0 to 7, double at offsets 8 to 15, age at offsets 16 to 19, four trailing padding bytes at offsets 20 to 23 so the size is a multiple of 8, total size still 24. Reordering removes the internal padding but not the trailing padding in this case, because the struct size must still round up to the largest alignment, 8. The lesson is that ordering largest to smallest removes internal waste, even when the total size stays the same because of trailing padding.
systems-22-lab.question: Design, on paper, a struct for a student record (name as a pointer, age, grade average) and draw its layout with padding, assuming 8-byte alignment for pointers and 8-byte doubles. Then reorder the fields to minimise padding and redraw.

systems-23.question: In your own words, distinguish use-after-free, double-free, and leak — and say which one a garbage collector prevents.
systems-23.correctAnswer: Use-after-free is using heap memory after it was freed, so reads return someone else's data and writes corrupt it. Double-free is freeing the same block twice, which corrupts the allocator's free-list. A leak is allocating without freeing, so a long-running program's memory grows until it is killed or the system slows. A garbage collector prevents use-after-free and double-free, because the programmer never frees memory by hand; it also reclaims memory that is no longer reachable, but it does not prevent a leak where a reference is still held even though the data is no longer needed.

systems-23.question: Predict why a buffer overflow might crash immediately in one program and silently corrupt data in another.
systems-23.correctAnswer: A buffer overflow writes past the end of a buffer into adjacent memory, and what happens depends on what sits next to it and whether that corrupted value is used. If it overwrites a return address, a saved register, or a pointer that is used straight away, the program crashes at or near the fault. If it overwrites data that is never read, is overwritten again before use, or only affects an output nobody checks, the corruption stays latent and the program keeps running with wrong data. Memory errors often do not crash at the faulty line; a corrupted value may be used much later, in unrelated code.

systems-23.question: Connect this to the next lesson: if memory errors are about where data lives, why does how a program accesses data affect its speed so much?
systems-23.correctAnswer: Because a processor is far faster than main memory, so speed depends on whether the data a program needs is already nearby in cache when it is asked for. Accessing data in an order that reuses nearby, recently used data keeps the cache working and the CPU fed; accessing data in a scattered order misses the cache constantly and pays the full trip to RAM each time. So where data lives, and the order it is visited in, decide performance even when the instruction count is the same.

systems-23-lab.question: For each error class above, write one sentence describing a program that commits it, and one sentence describing how you would detect it. No code is required — naming the error precisely is the skill being practised.
systems-23-lab.correctAnswer: Example set covering the lesson's error classes. Use-after-free: a program frees a message buffer and then prints from it; detect it with an address sanitizer, which reports the access to freed memory. Double-free: a program frees the same block on two error-handling paths; detect it with a sanitizer or allocator checker, which reports the second free. Buffer overflow: a program copies user input into a fixed buffer without checking its length and overwrites the neighbouring variable; detect it with a sanitizer or by fuzzing with over-long inputs. Buffer over-read: a program reads past the end of a buffer using a client-supplied length; detect it with a sanitizer or fuzzing. Leak: a server allocates a record per request and never frees it, so its memory grows over hours; detect it with a leak checker or by watching memory grow over time. Stack overflow: a function recurses with no base case until the stack is exhausted; detect it from the crash and the deep call stack. Uninitialised use: a program reads a variable it allocated but never wrote, getting whatever old data was there; detect it with a sanitizer that tracks uninitialised reads. Dangling pointer: a function returns a pointer to its own stack local and the caller uses it after the frame has returned; detect it with a sanitizer, which reports a stack-use-after-return.

systems-24.question: In your own words, explain why walking a row-major array column-by-column is slow, using cache lines.
systems-24.correctAnswer: In a row-major layout each row is stored contiguously, and a cache fetch brings in a whole line, neighbours included. Walking row by row uses every element of each fetched line before moving on, so most accesses are already cached. Walking column by column jumps by a whole row's width on every step, landing in a different cache line each time and using only one element from each line fetched, so nearly every access misses and pays the full trip to RAM. The same loops with the order swapped can differ by an order of magnitude in runtime.

systems-24.question: Predict the effect of doubling a program's working set beyond L3 cache size, and of halving it to fit in L1.
systems-24.correctAnswer: Doubling the working set beyond L3 cache size means the data a program actively uses no longer fits in any cache, so it thrashes: lines are evicted before they are reused, most accesses miss to RAM, and the program slows sharply. Halving the working set to fit in L1 means the data it actively uses sits in the smallest, fastest cache, so most accesses hit there and the program runs fast.

systems-24.question: Connect this to the next lesson: if one program's locality matters this much, what happens when two programs share a machine and its caches?
systems-24.correctAnswer: Two programs sharing a machine also share its caches, so each program's accesses can evict the other program's lines, destroying the locality each one relied on and slowing both down. On multiple cores the effect is worse: two cores writing to different variables that share one cache line cause that line to bounce between cores, called false sharing, even though the variables are independent. Shared caches also leak information through timing, so a performance fix that ignores isolation can become a security bug.

systems-24-lab.question: On paper, take a 4 by 4 grid of numbers stored row by row, with one cache line holding 4 numbers. Count how many cache lines are touched when you visit the grid row by row, and how many when you visit it column by column. Explain which order exploits spatial locality, and why the other order does not — no code or measurement is needed.
systems-24-lab.correctAnswer: Row by row: 4 cache lines touched, one per row, and each line is fully used, all 4 of its numbers visited before moving on. Column by column: 16 line visits, because every step lands in a different row's line and uses only one number from it before jumping away, so each column revisits all 4 lines. Row-by-row order exploits spatial locality, since data near used data is used soon and the whole fetched line pays off; column-by-column order does not, since it throws away the neighbours each fetch brought in and must reload the same lines again for the next column.

systems-25.question: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter starting at 10, without a lock. List every possible final value and explain, step by step, how the wrong one happens.
systems-25.correctAnswer: Possible final values: 11 and 12. The correct result, 12, happens when the two read-modify-write sequences do not overlap: one thread reads 10, adds 1, writes 11, then the other reads 11, adds 1, writes 12. The wrong result, 11, happens when both threads read before either writes: thread A reads 10, thread B reads 10, thread A writes 11, thread B writes 11. One update is lost because both threads worked from the same stale read.

systems-25.question: Explain what a critical section is, what a lock guarantees about it, and why a lock only works if every thread touching the data uses it.
systems-25.correctAnswer: A critical section is the stretch of code that touches shared data and must not be interleaved with another thread's critical section for the same data. A lock, also called a mutex, guards it: a thread must hold the lock to enter and must release it when it leaves, which makes the read-modify-write atomic, indivisible, as if it happened in a single instant, while other threads wait outside. A lock only works if every thread touching the data uses the same lock, because one thread that skips the lock breaks the protection for everyone, silently, by reading and writing the shared data while another thread is inside its critical section.

systems-25.question: State the four conditions for deadlock, and for each one, name a design rule that breaks it.
systems-25.correctAnswer: Mutual exclusion: a resource held by one thread at a time; break it by making the resource shareable where that is safe, so no exclusive hold is needed. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another; break it by taking all locks at once or none, so a thread never waits while holding. No preemption: a held resource cannot be taken away by force; break it by using timeouts, so a wait cannot last forever and the thread releases what it holds and retries. Circular wait: thread A waits for something thread B holds while thread B waits for something thread A holds; break it by always taking locks in the same order, so a cycle cannot form.

systems-25.question: Why can a race condition pass a thousand test runs and still fail in production? What does that imply about how you should argue that concurrent code is correct?
systems-25.correctAnswer: A race only shows up under one particular interleaving, and the interleaving depends on the scheduler, the number of cores, and the load on the machine, so a test run samples only a tiny fraction of the possible orderings and may pass a thousand times before the failing ordering arrives on a customer's machine under load. Bugs that vanish when you try to observe them, because logging or a debugger changes the timing, are called Heisenbugs. This implies testing can show that a bug exists but passing tests cannot prove that a race does not exist, so correctness has to be argued from the design: which shared data exists, which lock guards it, and whether every access honours that lock.

systems-25.question: Describe a TOCTOU flaw in your own words: what is checked, what changes, and what happens in the gap?
systems-25.correctAnswer: TOCTOU means time-of-check to time-of-use. A program checks a condition, for example whether a user is allowed, whether a file is safe, or whether an account has funds, and then acts on it, but another thread or process changes the thing between the check and the act. What is checked is the condition, what changes is the thing the check was about, and what happens in the gap is that the check was true when made and false when used, so the action goes ahead on a basis that no longer holds. Attackers deliberately try to win that race, repeating the attempt until the timing lines up in their favour, which is why security-critical checks and the actions they authorise must be atomic, under the same lock, with no gap.

systems-25-lab.question: On your own machine only. Do a paper simulation first — no code needed. Write a shared tally starting at 10. Play two workers, A and B, each following the steps "read the tally, add 1, write the tally back." Interleave their steps in three different orders, including one where both read before either writes. Record the final tally for each order and circle the lost update. Then, on your own machine only, open your operating system's process viewer and find a program with many threads; note how many threads it has and why a program that looks like "one app" is really many paths of execution sharing data. Write one sentence naming the shared data you think matters most in that program, and one sentence naming what a lock would protect there.
systems-25-lab.correctAnswer: Paper simulation, three orders. Order 1, A fully then B: A reads 10, writes 11, B reads 11, writes 12, final tally 12, no lost update. Order 2, B fully then A: B reads 10, writes 11, A reads 11, writes 12, final tally 12, no lost update. Order 3, both read before either writes: A reads 10, B reads 10, A writes 11, B writes 11, final tally 11, circle this lost update, one increment vanished because both workers used the same stale read. Process viewer part, worked example: a web browser may show dozens of threads across its processes, because one app is really many paths of execution, one per tab, one for networking, one for rendering, one for the interface, sharing data such as the tab list, the download list, or the open document. The shared data that matters most is the list of open tabs and pages, and a lock would protect that list while a thread adds, closes, or reads a tab, so two threads cannot update it at the same moment.

systems-26.correctAnswer: Process A has no address that names Process B's memory, because each process gets its own virtual address space, its own private view of memory as if it owned the whole machine. The hardware memory-management unit enforces this on every access, using page tables set up by the operating system: each process has its own page table mapping its virtual pages to physical pages, and only the kernel may change page tables. An ordinary bug in A therefore cannot read or corrupt B's data, because A's addresses simply do not translate to B's physical pages, unless memory has been deliberately shared by mapping the same physical pages into both address spaces.
systems-26.question: Explain, in your own words, why Process A cannot simply read Process B's memory, and name the hardware and operating-system mechanisms that enforce that.

systems-26.correctAnswer: Privilege is the level of authority a program runs at, such as user mode versus kernel mode, or an ordinary account versus an administrator account. Permission is whether a particular identity is allowed a particular operation on a particular resource, such as reading a specific file. Example of permission without privilege: an ordinary user program has permission to read its own file, but lacks the privilege to execute a privileged instruction, change page tables, or load a driver. Example of privilege without permission: a program running with elevated privilege, such as an administrator service, may still be denied a specific file if that file is encrypted with another user's key or protected by a sandbox that does not grant access to it, because elevation does not automatically grant the key or the sandbox permission. Note that on many systems a root account can bypass simple permission bits, so the clean distinction is processor mode and account authority versus per-resource permission checks, not that privilege always wins.
systems-26.question: What is the difference between privilege and permission? Give an example where a program has the permission it needs but lacks the privilege, and one where the reverse is true.

systems-26.correctAnswer: Step by step: first, a buffer overflow writes past the end of a buffer inside one program, overwriting adjacent memory, which may include control data such as a return address. That gives the attacker control of execution inside that program, crossing the memory-safety boundary. Next, the attacker uses that control to escape the program's sandbox or restricted environment, if any, crossing the isolation boundary into a more privileged process. Next, the attacker exploits a privilege-escalation flaw to run code in kernel mode or as administrator, crossing the privilege boundary. Finally, with kernel or administrator power, the attacker can read any memory, touch any device, install persistent malware, and disable protections, which is a full machine takeover. Each step crosses a different boundary: memory safety, then isolation, then privilege, then the whole system.
systems-26.question: Trace the chain from a buffer overflow to a full machine takeover, naming each boundary crossed at each step.

systems-26.correctAnswer: Initial flaw: an out-of-bounds write in the sandboxed renderer, a memory-safety error. First gain: control of execution or arbitrary write inside the renderer process, contained at first by the sandbox. Boundary crossed: the sandbox boundary, via the chained privilege-escalation flaw in the kernel, which lets the attacker run code in kernel mode. Final impact: full machine control, since kernel power can read any memory, touch any device, and bypass other protections. One layer that could have stopped each step: bounds checking, memory-safe code, or non-executable data pages for the renderer flaw; sandbox isolation and least privilege for the renderer gain; kernel patching, privilege separation, and layout randomisation for the kernel flaw; and monitoring, patching, and least-privilege permissions as a final layer around all of it.
systems-26.question: Read (in your head, from the description in this lesson) a vulnerability described as "an out-of-bounds write in a sandboxed renderer, chained with a privilege-escalation flaw in the kernel." Map it: initial flaw, first gain, boundary crossed, final impact, and one layer that could have stopped each step.

systems-26.correctAnswer: Because every single boundary can fail, and defence in depth is designed so that one failure is not fatal. Kernels have bugs, permissions are misconfigured, sandboxes have escapes, and hardware flaws have broken supposedly solid boundaries in real systems. Layering memory-safety mitigations, address-space isolation, privilege separation, permissions and sandboxing, and monitoring and patching means an attacker must cross several independent layers, not just one. A misconfigured layer costs you the protection that layer was supposed to provide, and worse, it can give false confidence: you believe you are protected, so you do not notice that one failure now leads straight to takeover, instead of being caught by the next layer.
systems-26.question: Why is defence in depth necessary even if you believe each individual boundary is strong? What does a misconfigured layer cost you?

systems-26-lab.correctAnswer: On your own machine or a class lab only. Reading and inspecting your own system is safe; never probe, test, or attempt to bypass protections on a system you do not own or are not authorised to test. Two reading-only exercises. First, on your own phone or computer only, list the permissions granted to three apps you actually use, and for each one, write whether it follows least privilege or asks for more than its job needs - and which permission you would remove if you could. Second, find a public vulnerability summary from a vendor advisory or reputable security news source (reading only - do not download exploits, do not test anything) and map it to boundaries using the four questions in the Technical Explanation: initial flaw, first gain, boundary crossed, and layers that could have stopped it. Write the map in four short lines. The expected pattern for the first exercise is: an app that only needs, for example, camera access for photos but also asks for contacts, location, and microphone is asking for more than its job needs, and the permission to remove is the one unrelated to its job. For the second exercise, the four lines should be: initial flaw, such as a memory error or misconfiguration; first gain, such as a read, write, or control inside the first program; boundary crossed, such as a sandbox escape or privilege escalation; and layers that could have stopped it, such as bounds checking, isolation, least privilege, or patching.
systems-26-lab.question: On your own machine or a class lab only. Reading and inspecting your own system is safe; never probe, test, or attempt to bypass protections on a system you do not own or are not authorised to test. Two reading-only exercises. First, on your own phone or computer only, list the permissions granted to three apps you actually use, and for each one, write whether it follows least privilege or asks for more than its job needs — and which permission you would remove if you could. Second, find a public vulnerability summary from a vendor advisory or reputable security news source (reading only — do not download exploits, do not test anything) and map it to boundaries using the four questions in the Technical Explanation: initial flaw, first gain, boundary crossed, and layers that could have stopped it. systems-27.correctAnswer: Three hypotheses, each with a supporting and a ruling-out measurement. Hypothesis 1, a runaway process: support is one process near 100 percent processor use while the symptom lasts; ruling out is processor use low or idle while the machine still feels slow. Hypothesis 2, memory full and swapping: support is memory near full, swap use active and growing, and a process whose memory grows steadily; ruling out is plenty of free memory and no swap use. Hypothesis 3, disk full or disk busy: support is a disk near full, or one process with constant heavy disk activity while the symptom lasts; ruling out is plenty of free disk space and low disk activity. Each hypothesis must be tested with its own predicted measurement, not by blaming the biggest number you happen to see.

systems-27.correctAnswer: Because tools show measurements, not diagnoses, and without a hypothesis you will pattern-match to whatever looks dramatic, whether or not it explains the symptom. Forming a hypothesis first forces you to predict what you should see if your theory is right, so a negative result can rule a theory out, which is just as valuable as a positive result confirming one. Opening tools first invites the classic beginner error of blaming the biggest number, even when that number is normal background work, while the real cause hides in an unglamorous column such as swap use.

systems-27.correctAnswer: Observing means reading the system without changing it, such as listing processes, reading memory and disk statistics, and reading logs. Changing means altering the system, such as ending a process, deleting files, changing settings, or restarting a service. The distinction matters more on a shared machine because changing can destroy another user's unsaved work, break a program other people depend on, or exceed your authority, while observing, done properly, does not affect other users at all. On your own machine, observe freely and change deliberately; on a machine you do not own or are not authorised to administer, do not change anything.

systems-27.correctAnswer: When memory is full, the system starts swapping, using disk as overflow memory because physical memory is full. Disk is orders of magnitude slower than memory, so every page fault that has to go to disk feels dramatically slower, and the machine slows all at once, not gradually. Buying a faster processor is the wrong fix because the processor is not the bottleneck: it is waiting for slow disk swaps, and a faster processor will simply wait faster. The fix is freeing memory, closing programs, or adding memory, so the system stops swapping.

What to check next is what that service is trying to do, why it keeps failing, and whether its activity correlates with processor, memory, or disk use at the slow time, and to read the log entries around the first occurrence for the original error, rather than just the repeated warnings.
